My brother came to my work the other day. I thought it was strange. He took me out front and told me my dad had passed away. For most this is crushing news, for me it sucked, just not as terrible. My father and I have been estranged for 8 years now. He was a raging alcoholic and he let is consume his life. We had 2 choices - watch it consume him or leave. He was also narcissistic and a drug abuser. He was never sober and when he did talk to us - he only wanted money or pity. This man threatened suicide weekly, was in and out of jail and rehab, a terrible womanizer, and an all around bad person. I posted this the other day - I think it sums up my relationship quite well:

"I suppose everyone else is talking about it, so I may as well jump on board. Last night around 8:30pm I found out my father had passed away. We have been estranged for almost 8 years if memory serves right and I honestly cannot remember the last time I saw him. With how everyone told me he was doing, I would likely not recognize him if I did.

When I was young I loved my dad, but I feared him. He had an insurmountable anger, which I regrettably inherited. He never once laid an ill hand on me or my siblings and I know that he loved us kids as much as he could. Childhood was not all bad - I remember a lot of trips to the zoo, fishing every Sunday, and him dragging us to Lowe's. He was a fantastic salesman and had quite the silver tongue. He was mostly talk, though.

After the passing of his mother, the decline happened. I can only recall a handful of times in which he was sober. Each year his actions and willpower rolled downhill. Still, we stood by him, he was our father after all. After a few years it became hard to support him. Every conversation resulted in "how can it benefit Dad?" Life continued for me and little by little dad fell out out of it. He occasionally came back with some promise of sobriety that was always fleeting. After about 100 second chances, I decided to cut the tether. Some might think me cruel for this, but a person can only take so much abuse.

He died as he lived - alone and drunk. He had pushed us all away so there is no closure. He was not invited to my wedding, he has not met his grandson, and he has not seen the man I have become today. I have a lot of mixed emotions right now. He was my dad and he's gone, but I know that if he had stayed in my life the past few years he would not have made it any better for either of us. I once heard that hell is meeting the person you could have become, and I think Dad faced hell every day. He had money, a large family, and a huge network of friends and co-workers. He threw it all away. There was no demon or disease - just a lack of willpower and foresight.

As weird as it sounds, I love him and miss him. Maybe because he was some master of manipulation, or maybe it is like a phantom limb. You left me and my siblings to find out everything for ourselves and set the perfect example of who not to be. Goodbye, Dad. I hope you find the peace in death that life could never afford you."

ValueWeb makes the contention that you cannot have an internet of things without a real-time and cheap internet of value. A core part of this is focused upon building a cheap shared ledger structure for digital identity and digital currencies and guess what? That cheap shared ledger is most likely going to be built in Africa. In fact, Devie Mohan of Thomson Reuters, one of the many fine speakers at Dot Finance, predicted that Africa would invent the global standard for digital identity and she may well be right.

After all, Africa cannot function as a continent if transactions are expensive and exclusive of citizens living on a dollar a day and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation have made it their priority to solve this problem. The Foundation is investing millions in Sub-Saharan Africa to solve this problem. Interestingly, some of those problems are now being solved by African Fintech start-up companies.
